The paper is an empirical evaluation along with proposals and directions for improving the field of time-series anomaly detection, with specific focus on deep models.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Recently, Wu & Keogh (2021) showed that it is hard to assess the benefit of new anomaly detection methods for (univariate) time series data. This is notably due to flawed benchmarks, inconsistent evaluation metrics, and protocols. This paper addresses these issues for multivariate time series data with deep learning methods. First, the most widely-used multivariate datasets are critically analyzed, which leads to the identification of multiple issues and the selection of the best candidates for evaluation. Second, a new "recall consistent" evaluation metric is proposed. Finally, the existing evaluation protocols are reviewed and a large benchmark of deep anomaly detection methods is proposed. The code to reproduce the experiments is provided in the supplementary material.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Similar to Wu & Keogh (2021), this analysis could valuable to the anomaly detection community going forward.
- A new "recall consistent" evaluation metric is proposed.
- A large benchmark of deep anomaly detection methods is provided.
- Overall, the paper is clear.


Weaknesses
- Proposing a new metric (in Section 4.2) along with the analysis makes it hard to read and evaluate the paper. I think sticking to the analysis would have made the paper stronger. 
- The paper focuses on point-wise anomaly detection.

Comments
- The discussion on recall consistency is too brief. Please provide a clear definition and more details.
- "Other papers have evaluated small selections of methods in a similar setting (Lai et al., 2021; Audibert et al., 2022)."
	- This sentence is too vague. You should provide more details. What do you mean by "small selections"? How small is it compared to your analysis?

- Typos:" hyperpparameters", "suffices show"

- In the appendix, what is P(|T|)?

- "To the best of our knowledge, there is no automatic statistical test to identify distributional shift in time series"
	- I think this statement is too strong. Finding distributional shifts is a fundamental statistical problem.
- When talking about Lemma 1 in the main text, please add a reference to the Appendix.
- Section 4.2, the case n=1 is written as gamma(n) instead of gamma(1).

content.title: Author Response to Review #2
content.comment:
The goal of our paper is to address the three most pervasive issues in anomaly detection on multivariate time series. As mentioned in our general comment above, we believe the metric and its theoretical motivation is an integral part of the presented work.
Even though some prior work is concerned with other settings in time-series anomaly detection, point-wise anomaly detection is the most common setting evaluated in almost all papers we reference in our work. It is a generally desirable setting, as in many real-world applications timely predictions are necessary for smooth operation. Furthermore, discontinuous predictions within continuous anomaly windows are inherently addressed within the metric we propose.

**Addressing the comments:**
- We acknowledge that a deeper discussion of recall consistency could help readability and will include the formal definition in the appendix.
- "small selections" refers to selections of generally less than five deep methods (not counting the shallow methods; in this context including the shallow methods would still only leave less than 16 methods) and we will include the exact numbers in the camera ready version.
- We thank you for pointing out grammatical and spelling errors which we will fix. We will also address your valid comments about Lemma 1 and the n=1 case.
- P([T]) refers to the power set of the set [T] = {1, ..., T} meaning the set of all subsets of [T].
- We agree that "Finding distributional shifts is a fundamental statistical problem". However, after an extensive literature search and consulting with experts, we were not able to find any work directly applicable to multivariate time-series data. If you are aware of work that we missed in that regard or some obvious application that we missed, we would be grateful if you could provide a reference. We are excited to extend our analysis in this direction in future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an experimental study of deep neural network methods for anomaly detection in time series. The paper discusses several shortcomings of existing solutions in that area, from flaws in datasets to problematic evaluation measures. The paper then proposes a new evaluation measure and proceeds with an evaluation of several DNN methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. Anomaly detection for time series is a timely and important problem
2. Well-written and motivated paper
3. Good effort for evaluation large number of DNN methods in that area

Weaknesses:

1. Missing several recent advances in the area, which invalidates part of the analysis
2. No thorough evaluation of evaluation measures
3. No comparison on sufficient large datasets

Comments:

- The paper attempts to resolve several important issues in the time-series anomaly detection literature. Unfortunately, there are recent advances in that area that have been completely omitted, which I believe invalidates the current work.

TSB-UAD [a] is recent, published well in-advance before ICLR submission, and establishes a new benchmark in that area while evaluating multiple methods including DNNs. The focus is on univariate time series but this really is irrelevant (the current work focus on multivariate and not univariate cases without justification - DNNs can easily work with univariate time series as well). Similarly, Schmidl et all also evaluated many DNN methods on both univariate and multivariate datasets, so the current work just seems as a selection of methods on just different set of datasets (it's somewhat obsolete in some sense as it's not really changing the landscape of what is known for solutions in that area. Focusing ONLY on DNN methods is also not properly justified, both TSB-UAD and Schmidl et all showed non-DNN methods to top the benchmarks.

VUS [b] also published well in-advance proposes new families of measures that solve issues discussed in this paper. Unfortunately, none of these papers are mentioned and without using them/comparing with them, it becomes impossible to evaluate the significance of the current work.

[a]  "Tsb-uad: an end-to-end benchmark suite for univariate time-series anomaly detection." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 15.8 (2022): 1697-1711.

[b] "Volume under the surface: a new accuracy evaluation measure for time-series anomaly detection." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 15.11 (2022): 2774-2787.

content.title: Author Response to Review #1 - 1
content.comment:
In the following, we will discuss the concerns one by one.

**1. Missing several recent advances in the area, which invalidates part of the analysis**

Here, you seem to have the two later-mentioned works [TSB-UAD] and [VUS] in mind. First, we would like to thank you for bringing these recent and indeed somewhat related papers that we were not aware of to our attention. It is an easy fix to include these papers in the related work discussion in the camera ready version. However, we strongly disagree with your statement that these papers render our contributions *"somewhat obsolete"* for the following reasons:

*Starting with [TSB-UAD]:*
TSB-UAD should be cited but its focus is benchmarking univariate time series AD methods while our work addresses the multivariate case. This is an important distinction for several reasons:
- The multivariate setting is important in practice. Take the simple example of electricity produced by a solar panel: A good method should detect that it is abnormal if an increase in sun intensity does not yield an increase in the electricity produced. Univariate methods can not capture these simple anomalies in the cross-correlation domain.
- In fact, many methods we consider in our study explicitly or implicitly rely on the correlation of features, for example by considering correlation matrices or utilizing feature-based graphs or attention mechanisms [MSCRED, GDN, GenAD]. Thus many methods are just not applicable to univariate data without compromising on large parts of the model and ignoring key aspects of the data. We provide the details and explanations of each method in the appendix, as these discussions would take away from the core message of the paper.
- The multivariate datasets considered in our study are among the largest, most complex, and widely used publicly available datasets in the field. Given the great acceptance of these datasets and that we, to the best of our knowledge, are the first ones who critically analyze these datasets, we believe in the novelty and usefulness of our work.
- It is well known that deep learning-based methods generally excel on large amounts of complex data. Furthermore, including and adapting the wide variety of shallow methods to our setting would greatly exceed the scope of this study since the comparison of different methods only makes up a small part of our study. Nevertheless, we agree that including shallow methods could be an interesting future research direction, so we are grateful for the remark.

*About [VUS]:*
This paper is somewhat closer related to our work, so we again thank you for bringing this paper to our attention. Nevertheless, by no means do we think this impairs our work for the following reason:
- The proposed VUS metrics cannot distinguish predictive patterns inside anomaly windows and thus carry over a crucial disadvantage of point-wise metrics. We discuss this flaw in section 3.2 of our paper.
- The proposed metrics heavily rely on extensions of anomaly windows to fix possible flaws in datasets and methods. Metrics should not be designed to compensate for actual problems in datasets. In our opinion, this makes the metrics in [VUS] inherently biased. Our proposed metric works without such extensions.
- Compared to our metric, the proposed metrics are far less flexible due to the omission of many relevant hyperparameters.
Therefore, despite the paper [VUS], we believe that our proposed metric is advantageous over the VUS metrics and thus valuable for the community.

On a side note, we also would like to mention that according to [VLDB](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/3551793.3551830) the discussed paper [VUS] was published in July 2022. Hence, we do not agree that this paper was published *"well in-advance"*. In fact, according to [ICLR guidelines](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2023/ReviewerGuide) this counts as *"very recent work"* that authors are not necessarily required to compare their current work with.

**2. No thorough evaluation of evaluation measures**

Detailed analysis and comparison of metrics is a complex task that would exceed the scope of this work. In the paper, we give an intuitive example of the performance of our measure alongside a theoretical justification. We believe, that in the scope of this work a theoretical justification heavily outweighs an experimental comparison, but a more in-depth analysis is sorely needed and should be considered for future work. Nonetheless, we plan to extend the discussion with further examples and experiments in the camera ready version.

content.title: Author Response to Review #1 - 2
content.comment:
**3. No comparison on sufficient large datasets**

We do not fully understand this point and would like to ask you for further clarification. Which datasets, in particular, are you missing in our work? As mentioned above, we considered the most widely used multivariate datasets in TSAD literature---MSL, SMAP, SMD, SWaT, and WADI---as well as the relatively recent Exathlon dataset as candidates for our evaluation. Due to several issues mentioned in Section 3.1 and discussed in detail in Appendix B, we decided to drop all of them except SMD and Exathlon. In case you are aware of other freely available datasets that should be part of the evaluation, we would be happy to include further analysis and perhaps benchmarks on those as well.

**Reference**

[TSB-UAD] John Paparrizos, Yuhao Kang, Paul Boniol, Ruey S. Tsay, Themis Palpanas, and Michael J. Franklin. "Tsb-uad: an end-to-end benchmark suite for univariate time-series anomaly detection". Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 15(8):1697–1711, 2022.

[VUS] John Paparrizos, Paul Boniol, Themis Palpanas, Ruey S. Tsay, Aaron Elmore, and Michael J. Franklin. "Volume under the surface: a new accuracy evaluation measure for time-series anomaly detection". Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 15(11):2774–2787, 2022.

[MSCRED] Chuxu Zhang, Dongjin Song, Yuncong Chen, Xinyang Feng, Cristian Lumezanu, Wei Cheng, Jingchao Ni, Bo Zong, Haifeng Chen, and Nitesh V Chawla. "A deep neural network for unsupervised anomaly detection and diagnosis in multivariate time series data". In Proceedings of the AAAI conference on artificial intelligence, volume 33, pp. 1409–1416, 2019.

[GDN] Ailin Deng and Bryan Hooi. "Graph neural network-based anomaly detection in multivariate time series". In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, volume 35, pp. 4027–4035, 2021.

[GenAD] Xiaolei Hua, Lin Zhu, Shenglin Zhang, Zeyan Li, Su Wang, Dong Zhou, Shuo Wang, and Chao Deng. "Genad: General representations of multivariate time seriesfor anomaly detection". arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.04250, 2022.

content.title: General Author Response
content.comment:
First and foremost, we would like to thank the reviewers for the time and effort they spend reading our paper and the valuable comments/suggestions we have received from them.
From the reviews, we think there might be some misunderstanding about the core message of our presented work.
Neither the benchmark itself nor the metric alone is the focus of this paper.
The goal of our paper is to address the three most pervasive issues in anomaly detection on multivariate time series and provide a solid foundation for future research:
- We identify several flaws in many of the most widely used multivariate time series datasets and present their first detailed analysis. We extend the analysis by Wu and Keogh [CBF] to multivariate data and their list of detrimental flaws, for example, to include distributional shifts.
- We identify several issues with previously used evaluation metrics, both point-wise and range-based. Building upon the metric proposed in [TSRec], we introduce a new metric (which is *not* a special case of the TS precision and recall metric, because a different definition of precision) and prove that it does not exhibit any of the flaws we identified.
- Many deep TSAD methods do not come with an official implementation and if they do, they are often using different software libraries (e.g. tensorflow, pytorch) and evaluation procedures/metrics, data preprocessing, etc. Our library offers a common platform and flexible building blocks for the development of new deep TSAD methods and provides procedures to compare them to existing methods in a meaningful and consistent benchmark.

The insights from this analysis shed new light on past evaluations and hopefully pave the way for future research.
We will attempt to clarify our writing and highlight the core message better and further add an extended discussion on future research directions.

[CBF] Renjie Wu and Eamonn Keogh. "Current time series anomaly detection benchmarks are flawed and are creating the illusion of progress". IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 2021.

[TSRec] Nesime Tatbul, Tae Jun Lee, Stan Zdonik, Mejbah Alam, and Justin Gottschlich. "Precision and recall for time series". Advances in neural information processing systems, 31, 2018.
